title: The Judas Priest Suicide Trial
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck cover the 1990 Judas Priest trial in Reno, Nevada, a product liability lawsuit alleging that subliminal backmasked messages in the song "Better By You, Better Than Me" led two fans, Raymond Belknap and James Vance, to a suicide pact in December 1985. The episode traces the Satanic Panic and backmasking background, the 1985 PMRC hearings, the Ozzy Osbourne "Suicide Solution" suit, the trial's plaintiff and defense arguments and expert witnesses, Judge Jerry Carr Whitehead's ruling for the band on invasion-of-privacy grounds, the CBS discovery sanction, Vance's later death, and the spread of the moral panic to rap music. Ends with a listener email about streaming music economics.
topics: Better By You Better Than Me

entities.name: Better By You, Better Than Me

segments.title: Opening and trigger warning
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode with a content warning for drug, alcohol and suicide references and recommend a Village Voice article, The Dreamer Deceiver by Ivan Solotaroff.

segments.title: Background: Satanic Panic and backmasking
segments.summary: Chuck explains the early-1980s Satanic Panic and backmasking, the idea of hidden messages heard when music plays backward. Josh points to the earlier Satanic Panic episode and the book chapter on backmasking.

segments.title: California AB 37-41 warning label bill
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck describe California assemblyman Phil Wyman's bill, prompted by a constituent who saw a Trinity Broadcast Network show, which claimed backmasked messages affect the subconscious. The bill was never voted on.

segments.title: Pseudoscience and expert witness William Yarrell
segments.summary: Hosts discuss William Yarrell's self-described neuroscience credentials and his claim that the unconscious decodes backmasked messages and acts on them, and how junk science gains traction.

segments.title: PMRC and 1985 congressional hearings
segments.summary: The Parents Music Resource Center and its proposed warning labels are discussed, along with the 1985 hearings featuring Frank Zappa and John Denver. Hosts reflect on the resulting Parental Advisory label and testimony such as Joe Stuckey's claims about scientific studies.

segments.title: Ozzy Osbourne suit and the Reno tragedy
segments.summary: The 1985 lawsuit against Ozzy Osbourne and CBS Records over Suicide Solution was dismissed on First Amendment grounds. In December 1985 in Reno, Nevada, Raymond Belknap and James Vance were best friends and Judas Priest fans; Belknap died by shotgun suicide after a day of drinking and marijuana.

segments.title: Vance's survival and the song Better By You, Better Than Me
segments.summary: Vance survived a shotgun suicide attempt, and in a letter to Belknap's mother he blamed alcohol and heavy metal, including Judas Priest. The boys believed the song Better By You, Better Than Me, a Gary Wright cover on Stained Class, contained 'do it' and other backmasked phrases. Chuck describes the song's original anti-war meaning.
topics: Better By You Better Than Me

segments.title: Product liability lawsuit and Judge Whitehead's jurisdiction
segments.summary: Attorney Ken McKenna's firm filed a product liability suit against Judas Priest and CBS Records. Judge Jerry Carr Whitehead in Washoe County heard it without a jury, and hosts explain why the subliminal-message framing was treated differently from protected lyrics.

segments.title: Families, band reaction and blame
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the parents' hostility toward the music, the band's distress at being blamed, and the troubled home lives of the boys, including the stepfather's alcoholism, and psychologist commentary about other risk factors.

segments.title: Plaintiff case: identifying, intent, subliminality
segments.summary: The plaintiffs needed to show an identifiable message, deliberate placement, subliminal nature, and capacity to cause suicide. Engineer William Nick Lough slowed and isolated the audio, and Wilson Key's subliminal advertising claims were used. Halford admitted the band had used backmasking before, for effect.

segments.title: Psychologist testimony on unconscious mind
segments.summary: Clinical psychologist Howard Shevrin testified about the conscious and unconscious mind and claimed subliminal messages can be perceived as internal truths. Hosts note the testimony went beyond the evidence, and that the judge's ruling covered only subliminal messages, not lyrics.

segments.title: Defense case and sound analysis
segments.summary: The defense argued that 'do it' was not clearly present, a combination of guitar and Halford exhaling, and used their own sound engineer. Halford explained his vocal habits. Defense cross-examined families, and experts testified there was no scientific basis for subliminal behavioral effects. Band members were distressed by the case.

segments.title: Ruling, invasion of privacy and damages
segments.summary: Judge Whitehead ruled for Judas Priest, treating the case as invasion of privacy requiring intent rather than product liability. He did not debunk subliminal messages, which later bolstered other claims. Judas Priest spent about a quarter million dollars on defense; CBS was ordered to pay $40,000 for discovery violations over the master tapes.

segments.title: Aftermath, Vance's later death and moral panic moves to rap
segments.summary: Vance later died after an overdose of methadone, with disputes over whether it was suicide. The panic shifted to rap, and Two Live Crew was tried for obscenity in Florida in 1990.

segments.title: Tour mention
segments.summary: Chuck notes Judas Priest's tour dates, including a September 21 show in Cedar Rapids, Iowa.

segments.title: Listener mail on streaming music
segments.summary: A listener named Nate from New York adds context on Spotify, label payouts to musicians and songwriters, and the power struggle between streaming services and labels.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to email the show and note the show's production credit.
